opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that this has happened over and over again throughout history. The great new technology and the bubble very often go together, because you can be completely right about the technology and still lose a lot of money on the investment. Think of the railroads, or the automobile and radio in the 1920s, or the internet in the late 1990s. Those technologies did change the world. But people got so excited that they bid the prices up too high and borrowed to do it, and when reality fell short of those expectations, the investments crashed even as the technology kept advancing.

So I separate two questions: Is the technology revolutionary? And is the investment a good one at that price? AI is, I believe, revolutionary. It will greatly raise productivity, but also create enormous disruption. That doesn't tell you whether the price is right, though. To judge that, I look at a few things. How high are prices relative to traditional measures, and are they discounting future earnings growth that's unlikely to materialize? Are there a lot of new buyers who have come in because they've seen prices go up? Is the sentiment broadly bullish? And most importantly, are those purchases being financed with debt?

Debt is the key, because a bubble doesn't burst just because people realize that prices are too high. It tends to burst when there's a need for cash. Wealth is not money. You can have a stock valued at a trillion dollars, but that isn't spending power until you sell it, and if everybody has to sell to get cash to service their debts, or pay their taxes, or meet some other obligation, then you get a mismatch between the amount of promised wealth and the amount of actual money. That's when the air comes out, and tight monetary policy or a wealth tax can be the pin that pricks it.

Right now, I see a lot of those bubble indicators flashing, though not all of them. That doesn't mean you should rush to sell, because a bubble can keep going for quite a while, and the last stretch can be very strong. But the risk is real, so I'd be careful about concentration, not assume that the great company of today is necessarily the winner at today's price, and make sure you're well diversified, including holding some things like gold that do well when the others don't. If you have a well-diversified portfolio, you don't have to predict exactly when the bubble will burst.

r001.rationale: It explains that excitement about revolutionary technology can drive investors to bid prices too high.

r002.rationale: It says the technology can change the world while investors still lose money because they paid too much.

r003.rationale: It links prices that assume earnings growth unlikely to materialize with reality falling short and investments crashing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that a revolutionary technology and a bubble are not mutually exclusive. In fact, they very often go together. If you look back through history, the railroads, electricity, the automobile, radio, the internet in the late nineties, every one of those changed the world, and every one of those also produced a bubble that wiped out a lot of investors. So the question isn't whether AI is real. It's real. The question is whether the prices being paid reflect a reasonable expectation of the cash flows that will come, and who is doing the buying, and with what money.

The way I think about a bubble is pretty mechanical. There are a handful of things I look at. Are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Are prices discounting unsustainable conditions, meaning they assume the growth rates of the last couple of years just continue indefinitely? Are there a lot of new buyers coming into the market who haven't been there before? Is there broad bullish sentiment, the kind where everybody at the dinner party is talking about it? Are purchases being financed with leverage, with borrowed money? And have companies or buyers made forward purchases, built out capacity, on the assumption that demand is going to be there? When you score those things, you get a sense of where you are. Today, on several of those measures, we're in bubble territory. Not on all of them, and not as extreme as 1929 or 2000, but the picture rhymes.

And here's the thing that trips people up. In a bubble, the technology does what everybody said it would do, and the investors still lose money. In 2000 the internet turned out to be more important than even the optimists thought, and yet most of the companies went to zero, because the winners were a small handful and the capital went everywhere. Being right about the technology and being right about the investment are two different things.

So what do I do about it? I don't try to call the top. Nobody can do that consistently, and a bubble can go on a lot longer than you think it should. What I do is diversify, and I make sure I'm not concentrated in the thing that everybody loves, and I pay very close attention to the credit side, because bubbles usually break when the money dries up, when interest rates rise or the financing isn't there to keep the game going. That's where I'd be watching. It's not the technology that breaks. It's the money.

r001.rationale: The response says revolutionary technology and bubbles often coincide, but does not explain that investors’ enthusiasm for the technology leads them to disregard the price they pay.

r002.rationale: It says the technology can deliver what investors expected while investors still lose money, and distinguishes being right about the technology from being right about the investment.

r003.rationale: The response identifies drying-up money, rising rates, and unavailable financing as ways bubbles break; it does not identify profits failing to justify stock prices as a reversal trigger.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: Is this technology going to change the world? And is this investment going to give you a good return at the price you’re paying? Those are very different questions.

You can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money. The excitement about something revolutionary leads people to extrapolate. They see extraordinary possibilities, prices go up, and the rising prices seem to confirm the story. More money comes in. Then the price can begin to imply a future that even a very successful business will have difficulty delivering.

So I would work backward from the price. What earnings would have to materialize to justify it? Who actually captures those earnings? Does competition drive down prices? Does the technology benefit customers enormously while making relatively little money for the companies providing it?

And then there’s the financing. If people have borrowed heavily to buy those assets, a disappointment can force selling, which creates another round of declines.

You don’t have to deny the importance of AI to recognize that risk. You have to distinguish the promise of the technology from what’s already reflected in the price, and construct your portfolio so that being wrong doesn’t knock you out of the game.

r001.rationale: It says revolutionary excitement leads investors to extrapolate possibilities and drive prices up, while emphasizing the need to assess the price paid.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says investors can be right about the technology and still lose money, and that even a successful business may struggle to deliver what its price implies.

r003.rationale: It asks what earnings would justify the price, but does not clearly identify earnings failing to justify stock prices as a trigger for the bubble’s reversal.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate two questions: Is this technology going to change the world? And is the price you’re paying for an investment justified? Those are very different questions. You can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money on the investment.

A revolutionary technology creates excitement, and that excitement attracts capital. Prices rise, people see other people making money, and they become afraid of missing out. Then the price begins to assume an extraordinary future. The risk is that even a very good future may fall short of what’s already priced in.

So I would look at the expectations embedded in prices, how much borrowing is financing the investment, and who will actually capture the profits. A technology can create tremendous benefits for society while competition makes it difficult for individual companies to earn attractive returns.

You also have to be humble about timing. Recognizing a bubble doesn’t tell you when it will end. The practical question is: If your assumptions are wrong, can you withstand the loss? You don’t want your financial well-being to depend on one compelling story.

r001.rationale: It explains that revolutionary technology creates excitement, draws capital, and pushes prices to assume an extraordinary future, capturing how enthusiasm can eclipse price concerns.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says investors can be right about the technology and still lose money because the investment price may not be justified.

r003.rationale: It discusses profit capture and expectations falling short, but does not identify profits failing to justify stock prices as a trigger for the bubble’s reversal.
